title: Indexing
subtitle: Internal mechanics of B+ Trees, LSM-Trees, composite index prefix rules, and covering indexes.
keyTakeaways: B+ Trees store data pointers only in leaf nodes linked sequentially, delivering O(log N) point lookups and fast range scans.
LSM-Trees (Log-Structured Merge-Trees) turn random disk writes into sequential append-only writes in MemTables and SSTables.
Composite indexes follow the leftmost prefix rule: an index on (A, B, C) accelerates queries on (A) and (A, B), but cannot be used for (B, C) alone.

sections.heading: 1. Architectural Fundamentals & Core Mechanics
sections.body: Indexing is a foundational architectural concept in distributed systems. Internal mechanics of B+ Trees, LSM-Trees, composite index prefix rules, and covering indexes. Fundamentally, B+ Trees (used by PostgreSQL and MySQL InnoDB) maintain balanced pages on disk (typically 8KB–16KB) with high fanout (hundreds of keys per node). A 3- to 4-level B+ Tree can index billions of rows while keeping internal nodes cached in RAM, requiring at most 1 disk I/O per lookup. Conversely, LSM-Trees (RocksDB, Cassandra) buffer writes in an in-memory red-black/skip-list (`MemTable`) and a disk `WAL`, flushing immutable sorted `SSTables` and compacting them in the background.
bullets: **Core Architectural Principle**: B+ Trees store data pointers only in leaf nodes linked sequentially, delivering O(log N) point lookups and fast range scans.
**Problem Space & Invariants**: LSM-Trees (Log-Structured Merge-Trees) turn random disk writes into sequential append-only writes in MemTables and SSTables.
**System Boundary**: Operates across client network dispatch, gateway queuing, thread execution pools, and persistent storage I/O.

sections.heading: 2. Architectural Patterns & Implementation Topologies
sections.body: In production distributed systems, indexing manifests across several distinct architectural classifications, operational modes, and implementation strategies:
bullets: **B+ Tree Storage Engine (PostgreSQL, InnoDB)**: Focuses on predictable low-latency reads, fast range scans, minimal read amplification. Best suited for Read-heavy OLTP workloads requiring low p99 read latency..

**LSM-Tree Storage Engine (RocksDB, Cassandra)**: Focuses on sequential disk writes yield massive ingestion throughput and better compression. Best suited for Write-intensive workloads like event logs, messaging, and time-series metrics..
Clustered Index (InnoDB Primary Key): Leaf nodes hold the actual row payload; secondary indexes store the primary key value, requiring a second lookup ('bookmark lookup') unless covered.
Heap Table (PostgreSQL): All indexes are secondary and point to `ctid` (physical page and tuple offset) in the heap.
Equality Before Range: In composite indexes, always order equality predicates (`=`) before inequality or range predicates (`>`, `<`, `BETWEEN`).
GIN / Inverted Indexes: Used for full-text search and JSONB containment queries where keys map to posting lists of row IDs.

codeSnippet.title: Composite & Covering Index Optimization in PostgreSQL
codeSnippet.code:
-- Slow query: filters by status & created_at, fetches amount
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT id, amount_cents FROM payments
WHERE merchant_id = 'm_42' AND status = 'SETTLED'
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;

-- Optimal Covering Index (Index-Only Scan, 0 heap fetches):
-- Equality columns first (merchant_id, status), then sort/range column (created_at),
-- and INCLUDE payload columns to avoid touching the table heap.
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_payments_merch_status_created
ON payments (merchant_id, status, created_at DESC)
INCLUDE (id, amount_cents);

sections.heading: 3. Production Strengths: Where & How to Apply
sections.body: Adopting appropriate design patterns around indexing unlocks critical performance, scalability, and operational advantages for modern backend platforms:
bullets: **Where to Use — High-Impact Scenarios**: Optimal for Read-heavy OLTP workloads requiring low p99 read latency. and environments requiring Predictable low-latency reads, fast range scans, minimal read amplification..

**Where to Use — High-Throughput Scenarios**: Recommended for Write-intensive workloads like event logs, messaging, and time-series metrics. where Sequential disk writes yield massive ingestion throughput and better compression..

**How to Use — Engineering Implementation**: Every additional index speeds up matching `SELECT` queries but slows down `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` operations because the storage engine must update every affected B+ Tree and risk page splits. Always establish explicit thresholds, measurement baselines, and automated monitoring.
**Architectural Leverage**: Provides predictable resource boundaries, bounds blast radius, and optimizes cost per transaction.

sections.heading: 4. Failure Modes & Trade-Offs: When to Avoid
sections.body: While essential for scalable engineering, indexing introduces substantial architectural trade-offs, operational failure modes, and anti-patterns if applied inappropriately:
bullets: **Where to Avoid — Trade-Off Bottlenecks**: Avoid when constraints impose random i/o on writes due to in-place page updates and page splits.
**Where to Avoid — Complexity Ceiling**: Avoid premature optimization when read amplification (checking multiple sstables) and compaction cpu/io spikes.
**Catastrophic Failure Modes**: Uncalibrated parameters can trigger queue exhaustion, thread starvation, cascading retry storms, and tail latency amplification.
**Operational Overhead**: Requires continuous observability (p95/p99 latency tracking, saturation alerts, and distributed tracing across hop boundaries).

sections.heading: 5. Staff+ Engineering Verdict & Interview Playbook
sections.body: Mastering indexing is a defining trait of Staff-level distributed systems engineers. Navigating the delicate balance between performance, reliability, and simplicity ensures architectures scale sustainably without introducing unmanageable operational friction.
bullets: **Staff+ Golden Rule**: Composite indexes follow the leftmost prefix rule: an index on (A, B, C) accelerates queries on (A) and (A, B), but cannot be used for (B, C) alone.
**Staff+ Interview Playbook**: When designing composite indexes in an interview, state the ESR rule explicitly: Equality columns first, Sort columns second, and Range/Included columns last.
